reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that effective fielding practice requires balancing two competing objectives: maximizing exposure to varied ball types and minimizing redundant effort. The first primitive, Ball Distribution Optimization, formalizes this as a stochastic allocation problem where the number of balls B must be optimally spread among F fielders to avoid underuse or overwork. This is modeled as a probabilistic assignment with catch success rate C as a latent variable. The second primitive, Batter Skill Variety, introduces a combinatorial constraint on hit types H_i that must span a range of kinematic features to train different fielder responses. These are linked through a shared objective function that maximizes information gain per ball. The third primitive, Turn Scheduling Protocol, addresses resource contention by modeling group dynamics as a discrete-time process. It ensures that N candidates rotate through practice phases without idle time, forming a temporal schedule that aligns with the physical limits of fielder endurance and attention. The interplay between these primitives creates a dual structure: one optimizing for information content (variety), the other for operational efficiency (turns). Failure modes include over-reliance on single hit types (reducing V), or inefficient scheduling (increasing T beyond P/N). The system's robustness depends on maintaining a balance between these dualities.
